A clinic can offer a costly cure to a few hepatitis C patients or screening to thousands. How to allocate?
A doctor can give extra time and free samples to a sympathetic patient, leaving less for others equally in need. Is favoritism justified?
A transplant committee weighs giving a liver to a patient who relapsed into drinking versus a first-time candidate. How to be fair and beneficent?
A physician can write off one uninsured patient's large bill, but doing so routinely would jeopardize care for all. What is right?
A sponsor offers funding only if the team excludes hard-to-treat patients who most need help. Accept to do some good, or refuse for fairness?
A hospital can install one expensive robot benefiting a few surgical patients or upgrade basic equipment used by all. Which serves ethics?
A doctor in a refugee camp can intensively treat a few critical patients or spread thin care across many. How to choose?
A clinic must decide whether to keep a no-show-prone but very sick patient in a limited program over reliable patients who would also benefit.
A physician can prescribe an off-label drug that may help her patient but, if widely copied, would strain shared formulary resources. Prescribe?
A bodybuilder asks his physician to monitor his self-prescribed anabolic steroids rather than refuse involvement. Harm-reduction or decline?
A patient insists on a dangerous crash diet before bariatric surgery against advice. Proceed on his terms or refuse?
A patient with factitious disorder demands invasive tests he does not need; refusing may send him elsewhere. What to do?
A long-term smoker awaiting lung resection refuses to quit. Should the surgeon make cessation a condition of operating?
A patient insists on a home birth after a prior emergency cesarean, against strong advice. Attend or refuse?
A patient wants to return to contact sport after a concussion despite second-impact risk. Clear him?
A patient demands a rapid opioid detox he has been warned is dangerous. Provide on his insistence?
A transplant recipient wants to stop immunosuppressants he finds intolerable, risking rejection. Respect his choice?
A patient refuses cardiac monitoring and signs out during an evolving heart attack. How far to intervene?
A patient with capacity refuses all pain relief to stay sharp while visibly suffering. Respect or keep persuading?
A patient wants to drive long-distance days after a seizure, below the legal seizure-free interval, and asks the doctor to stay silent. Respect autonomy?
A patient demands removal of a cast he finds unbearable before the fracture has healed, accepting deformity. Comply?
A patient insists on keeping a high-salt diet that worsens his heart failure and asks the dietitian to stop nagging. Set limits?
A patient prefers acupuncture over proven physiotherapy the physician thinks recovery needs. Support the choice?
A patient declines statins after a heart attack, citing internet fears, against clear benefit. Keep urging or accept?
A patient wants to stop a working antidepressant because he should manage without pills. Facilitate the taper or resist?
A patient asks his surgeon to do a smaller, less effective operation to shorten recovery, against best advice. Accommodate?
A patient with curable testicular cancer wants to delay treatment to take a trip. Accept the risk or push?
A patient refuses a hearing aid that would clearly help, finding it embarrassing. Where is the balance?
A patient wants to leave rehab early to return to work, jeopardizing recovery. Facilitate his wish?
A patient asks not to be screened for depression he suspects he has, preferring not to know. Honor the boundary?
A patient insists on a riskier open surgery over a recommended minimally invasive one for personal reasons. Proceed?
A patient declines anticoagulation after a clot, fearing bleeding, against strong benefit. Respect or persist?
A patient wants to keep breastfeeding on a drug that may harm the infant but helps her; she has weighed it. Support her choice?
A capacitated patient refuses a colostomy that would prevent recurrent obstruction, accepting repeated hospitalizations. Accept?
A patient demands proton-beam therapy when standard radiation is equally effective for his cancer. Order it on request?
A patient insists on weekly physiotherapy beyond clinical need while others wait months for a first slot. Accommodate?
A patient wants a costly continuous glucose monitor he could manage without, when budgets are tight. Prescribe on demand?
A patient requests transfer to a tertiary center for care a local hospital could provide, straining specialist beds. Honor?
A patient demands repeat imaging just in case, using scarce resources and radiation with no indication. Order it?
A patient wants the newest, priciest insulin when an older one works well for him and frees funds for others. Prescribe?
A patient demands a home-care package beyond his needs that others need more. How to respond?
A patient wants priority booking because he is busy and important, displacing others. Honor?
A patient insists on continued expensive monitoring after recovery for reassurance, tying up clinic capacity. Accommodate?
A patient requests an elective scan abroad billed to his insurer at high cost without indication. Support it?
A patient wants a private ambulance transfer at public expense for non-urgent reasons. Honor the preference?
A patient demands the senior consultant personally perform a routine procedure a trainee could do, reducing access for complex cases. Honor?
A vascular surgeon weighs an aneurysm repair that could prevent rupture but carries high operative mortality in a frail patient. Operate?
An oncologist considers immunotherapy that may cure but can cause fatal autoimmune organ failure. Offer it?
A cardiologist weighs an LVAD that could prolong life but risks stroke and infection. Recommend?
A nephrologist considers a living-donor transplant that helps the recipient but subjects a healthy donor to surgical risk. How to weigh harm to the donor?
A surgeon considers debulking a tumor that may relieve symptoms but could hasten death in a weak patient. Proceed?
An anesthesiologist weighs a regional block that improves recovery but risks rare permanent nerve injury. Recommend?
A maternal-fetal specialist weighs in-utero surgery that might save the fetus but endangers the mother. How to balance?
A pulmonologist considers a lung biopsy that could guide treatment but risks fatal hemorrhage. Order it?
A gastroenterologist weighs a stent that relieves obstruction but may perforate the bowel. Proceed?
An endocrinologist considers tight glucose control that improves outcomes but risks dangerous hypoglycemia in an elderly patient. How tight to aim?
An oncologist weighs radiation that could control a brain tumor but may cause lasting cognitive decline. Recommend?
A surgeon considers a high-risk reoperation that could fix a failed repair but may kill an already weakened patient. Proceed?
A clinician learns a daycare-worker patient has an untreated contagious infection and will not take leave. Report to protect children?
A physician must decide whether to disclose a soldier patient's PTSD that could affect unit safety, against confidentiality.
A physician treating both spouses learns one has an STI he refuses to disclose to the other, also his patient. What to do?
A clinician suspects a patient is diverting the controlled drugs she prescribes to vulnerable others. Report or protect privacy?
A doctor learns a patient plans to travel while infectious with measles. Notify public health against his wishes?
A psychiatrist's patient reveals ongoing violence toward children in the home. Breach confidentiality to protect them?
A clinician discovers a school-bus driver patient is misusing sedatives. Report despite ending his employment?
A genetic counselor learns a sperm donor carries a serious heritable disease affecting many offspring. Pursue notification against his wishes?
A physician treating a patient with recurrent arson impulses must weigh warning authorities against confidentiality.
A clinician must decide whether to enter a stigmatizing diagnosis in a shared record that protects other providers but exposes the patient.
During an epidemic, a clinician must decide whether to override a patient's refusal of contact tracing that endangers others.
A physician treating a public official learns of a condition the public has a safety interest in. Disclose or protect privacy?
A doctor must weigh reporting a patient's confessed plan to harm a specific ex-partner against the therapeutic relationship.
A physician must decide whether to spend scarce clinic hours on one complex case or a community screening day that helps many.
A drug is available through a compassionate-use lottery; should the physician lobby hard for her patient over equally deserving others?
A hospital weighs funding a NICU cot that saves few high-cost infants or maternity care improving many births. Which is ethical?
A doctor can offer a grateful patient priority follow-up as thanks, at the cost of others' access. Justified?
An ICU must decide between continuing care for a slowly improving long-stay patient and admitting several acute patients waiting.
A clinic can adopt an expensive diagnostic benefiting a rare subgroup or invest in basic care for the common majority. Which is right?
A transplant team weighs social-value criteria that maximize societal benefit against equal treatment of all candidates.
A hospital must decide whether to treat a wealthy medical tourist whose fees fund local care but who displaces local patients.
A physician must choose between intensive support for one premature infant and adequate staffing for the whole nursery.
A clinic must decide whether to keep funding a high-cost therapy for a few long-term patients or open access to new ones.
A doctor can give extra unbilled time to a struggling patient, but doing so for all would collapse the practice. What is right?
A physician can prioritize her dying patient's wish for a costly home setup that others equally need. How to allocate?
A pharmacy with limited stock must choose between filling one patient's large chronic order and reserving supply for many acute needs.
